newsitem.title: USA: U.S. feedlot cattle prices seen firm into spring.
newsitem.headline: U.S. feedlot cattle prices seen firm into spring.

text.p: U.S. feedlot cattle prices have made winter lows and should remain firm, possibly rising to $70.00 per cwt by spring because of recent winter storms and light weights, market analysts and feedlot sources said.

"Cattle from central Nebraska northward have been slowed down significantly by less than optimal feeding conditions since the early winter in that region," said Andy Gottschalk, livestock analyst with LFG.
Gottschalk said the storm that slammed into the southern Plains this past week set cattle gains back and prompted him to expand his bullish price outlook.
"I think there's a reasonable chance that the winter low in in place and I continue to look for a spring high in mid-March or mid-April at $70.00," Gottschalk said.
Dale Benson, Chicago-based analyst with Dean Witter Reynolds, said fed cattle prices into April could range from $64.00 to $68.00, but he said he would not be surprised to see $70.00.
Feedlot cattle in the U.S. Plains this week traded actively at $66.00 per cwt after dipping to $64.00 earlier this month, the lowest price this winter.

Cattle prices could slip occasionally as retailers periodically switch to pork for advertising features, especially if pork output surges the next few weeks as hogs held back by recent storms flood the market, Dean Witter's Benson said.
"Although beef features were currently running strong, lower priced pork could cut into beef promotions by early February," he said.

Extreme cold, windy conditions the past week in the Texas Panhandle and western Oklahoma area set cattle back for the first time this winter, said Jim Gill, market director of the Texas Cattle Feeders Association.
"This is the first week we saw weigh-ups lighter than they should have been, by as much as 20 lbs lighter (per head)," Gill said.
However, he said, moderating temperatures this weekend should put cattle back in a feeding mood.
Temperatures in the Texas Panhandle were expected to climb to 60 degrees Fahrenheit by Sunday from 14 F early Friday.

Benson said weight gains on cattle were set back seven to 10 days by the cold in the Panhandle area but as much as 30 days in Nebraska and the Dakotas, which have been besieged by winter storms since mid-December.

"They'll still be marketed on time but at sharply-reduced weights," Benson said. He said cattle weights have been running 20 to 30 lbs lighter than a year ago because of the recent cold and on strong beef demand has kept packers kept buying cattle ahead of schedule.

Average estimated weights of cattle slaughtered under federal inspection the week ended January 11 were pegged by the U.S. Agriculture Department at 1,162 lbs, slightly down from an estimated 1,163 the previous week and sharply below the actual average weight of 1,198 a year ago, USDA said.
Benson added that it probably will be May before aggressive placements and warmer weather bring cattle weights back to year-ago levels.
Light weights, in conjunction with a reduction in cow slaughter from a year ago has reduced beef production, analysts said.
Last week's production was a good example of the impact light-weight cattle had on beef production, Gottschalk said.

"We killed 19,000 more cattle and produced 1.8 percent less beef (for the week ended January 1), Gottschalk said. "We will produce less beef going into the spring because of the dramatic difference in weights, and that weight differential is being compounded now by the adverse weather," Gottschalk said.
